newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese company stands tough in tax dispute.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese company stands tough in tax dispute.

text.p: Lebanon's biggest cement company Societe des Ciments Libanais said on Thursday it was not prepared to back down in a $5 million tax dispute with the finance ministry.

Chairman Thomas Schmidheiny, who also heads SCL's parent company, Swiss-based multinational Holderbank, said the dispute over taxes and penalties demanded by the ministry for 1992 and 1993 involved a matter of principle.
"We are not prepared to give in because it's a very healthy amount, about $5 million," Schmidheiny told shareholders at their annual meeting at SCL's headquarters at Chekka, north of Beirut.
SCL is Lebanon's second biggest non-banking company and one of four industrials listed on the Beirut Stock Exchange.

The dispute hit its 1996 profits and dividend, which were announced at Thursday's meeting, causing a 33.5 percent decline in net profits to 14.993 billion Lebanese pounds from 22.533 billion in 1995 and postponement of the dividend payment.

After-tax profits before a provision set aside for the disputed 1992 and 1993 charges of 7.899 billion Lebanese pounds ($5.1 million) were 22.893 billion pounds -- 20 percent up from 19.025 billion in 1995.
Because of the dispute, the shareholders voted to freeze payment of a 37 pounds (2.4 cents) dividend.
They authorised the board to decide when it should be paid after Schmidheiny told them SCL would be unable to pay the dividend if it also had to pay the taxes and penalties.

Schmidheiny said in the annual report that the charges arose from the finance ministry's refusal to accept items in SCL's 1992 and 1993 "Raw materials and consumer goods" accounts as tax deductible and demanded that they be amortised over three years.
The ministry had failed to respond to arguments opposing its demand that SCL presented in 1995, he said.

"We maintain our opposition because the ministry's demand constitutes an astonishing change in fiscal policy which runs counter to the accounting principles adopted and applied until now in Lebanon and other countries of the world," Schmidheiny said.
"One cannot accept to capitalise and amortise over three years 'Raw materials and consumer goods'," he added.
The board refused to accept a compromise envisaged in the 1997 budget law under which the government could cancel up to 90 percent of the penalties, his report said.

Questioned by the shareholders about the taxes and penalties demanded by the finance ministry, Schmidheiny told the meeting: "It's unbelievable. This has not happened to us in any of the 40 countries we work in. We don't understand why it happened."
